title: The Presbyond/PresbyLASIK Prism: Blended Vision for Presbyopia
summary: PresbyLASIK, particularly advanced techniques like Presbyond, offers a corneal laser refractive solution for presbyopia. By creating extended depth of focus (EDOF) and/or micro-monovision profiles on the cornea, it aims to reduce or eliminate the need for reading glasses, providing functional vision across distance, intermediate, and near ranges.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on near objects due to hardening of the crystalline lens and weakening of the ciliary muscle. PresbyLASIK is an excimer laser corneal refractive procedure designed to correct presbyopia by creating extended depth of focus (EDOF) profiles or multifocal zones on the cornea. Unlike traditional monovision, which relies on a clear distance eye and a clear near eye, PresbyLASIK (e.g., Presbyond) aims for a 'blended vision' by subtly modifying the corneal shape, achieving a continuous range of vision across distance, intermediate, and near without significant monocular blur.

sections.title: Risk Factors for Presbyopia
content: Age (primary factor, typically 40-45 years)
Hyperopia (often leads to earlier onset)
Certain medications (e.g., anticholinergics, diuretics, antidepressants)
Systemic diseases (e.g., diabetes, anemia, cardiovascular disease)
Gender (some studies suggest slightly earlier onset in females)

branches: - Lens Growth (alters anterior chamber depth, affects focal point)
- Dominant Eye: Optimized for Distance (often plano to -0.25D myopia) with slight prolate asphericity.
- Non-Dominant Eye: Optimized for Intermediate/Near (e.g., -1.25D to -1.75D myopia) with increased negative spherical aberration (more steep centrally).
- Blended Vision Zone: Overlapping EDOF regions for seamless transition, promoting neuroadaptation.

rows: Asymmetric monovision with enhanced spherical aberration for depth of focus in each eye, creating a continuous blended zone.
Modifies corneal asphericity (Q-factor) to create a central near zone and peripheral distance zone in the non-dominant eye, maintaining distance in dominant.
Creates a central multifocal zone, often with an intermediate/near focus, blending into a distance periphery.
One eye corrected for distance (plano), the other for near (-1.50D to -2.00D myopia). No specific multifocal corneal sculpting.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features of Presbyopia (Pre-Treatment)
content: Difficulty reading small print or seeing objects up close (e.g., phone, books).
Need to hold reading material at arm's length (presbyopic 'long arm').
Eyestrain, headache, or fatigue during prolonged near work.
Blurred vision at intermediate distances.
Improvement in visual clarity for near tasks in bright light (due to pupil constriction).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination & Patient Selection
content: 1. Comprehensive Refraction: Manifest and Cycloplegic to determine spherical equivalent, cylinder, axis, and accommodative amplitude.
2. Best Corrected Visual Acuity: Distance (Snellen) and Near (Jaeger, N-notation) for both monocular and binocular vision.
3. Corneal Topography/Tomography: Rule out ectatic diseases (e.g., keratoconus, FFKC), assess corneal regularity, and central/peripheral pachymetry.
4. Ocular Aberrometry: Evaluate higher-order aberrations (HOAs) that might impact visual quality, especially contrast.
5. Ocular Dominance Determination: Essential for assigning distance/near correction (e.g., Hole-in-Hand test, Plus Lens blur test).
6. Pupilometry: Measure mesopic pupil size to assess potential for glare/haloes, especially with multifocal profiles.
7. Dry Eye Assessment: Schirmer test, Tear Break-up Time (TBUT), Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) questionnaire. Crucial for post-op comfort and visual quality.
8. Anterior Segment/Posterior Segment Exam: Rule out other pathologies (e.g., cataract, glaucoma, retinal disease).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Patient Counseling & Informed Consent: Thorough discussion of benefits, risks, alternatives, and realistic expectations (e.g., potential need for glasses for fine print).
2. Pre-Operative Dry Eye Management: Initiate artificial tears (e.g., Systane Ultra QID), topical cyclosporine/lifitegrast, punctal plugs if indicated, for 2-4 weeks prior.
3. Surgical Planning: Based on refraction, topography, dominance, and chosen PresbyLASIK platform, determine specific ablation profiles for each eye.
4. Femtosecond Laser Flap Creation: (e.g., Schwind ATOS, VisuMax, Intralase iFS) Create a superiorly hinged or nasal hinged corneal flap (90-110 µm thickness, 8.5-9.0 mm diameter).
5. Excimer Laser Ablation: Lift flap, apply customized PresbyLASIK (e.g., Presbyond) EDOF/multifocal ablation profile to stromal bed (e.g., Schwind AMARIS 1050RS).
6. Flap Repositioning: Rinse stromal bed, carefully reposition flap, ensure proper alignment, dry edges with a merocel sponge.
7. Post-Operative Medications: Topical antibiotic (e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID x 1 week) and topical steroid (e.g., Pred Forte 1% QID tapering over 2-4 weeks), preservative-free artificial tears.
8. Follow-up Schedule: Day 1, Week 1, Month 1, Month 3, Month 6, Year 1 to monitor healing, refraction, and visual quality.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Presbyond Example
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia: Apply anesthetic drops (e.g., Proparacaine 0.5%).
2. Eyelid Speculum: Insert to maintain globe exposure.
3. Femtosecond Laser Flap Creation: Dock patient, create corneal flap (e.g., 100µm thick, 9.0mm diameter) using femtosecond laser (e.g., Schwind ATOS).

4. Flap Lift & Excimer Laser Ablation: Gently lift flap with a blunt spatula. Position patient under excimer laser (Schwind AMARIS 1050RS). Eye tracking activated. Apply custom Presbyond SmartSurfACE ablation profile.
5. Flap Repositioning: Rinse stromal bed with balanced salt solution, carefully reposition flap, ensure no striae or debris, dry flap edges.
6. Post-op Drops: Administer antibiotic and steroid drops.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Dry Eye Syndrome: Most common post-op complaint, often transient but can be chronic.
Glare, Halos, Starbursts: Especially at night, due to induced spherical aberration; typically diminish with neuroadaptation.
Reduced Contrast Sensitivity: Can occur, impacting vision in low light conditions.
Ghosting/Diplopia: Can occur, especially in early post-op period or if neuroadaptation is poor.
Regression of Effect: Gradual loss of near vision over time, requiring enhancement or reading glasses.
Decentration of Ablation: Can lead to significant visual disturbances.
Flap Complications: Striae, epithelial ingrowth, diffuse lamellar keratitis (DLK).
Residual Refractive Error: Under- or over-correction, requiring glasses or enhancement.
Need for Reading Glasses: For very fine print or prolonged near work, even after successful surgery.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Contraindications for PresbyLASIK
content: Keratoconus or Forme Fruste Keratoconus (FFKC)
Insufficient Corneal Thickness (<480 µm residual stromal bed)
Unstable Refraction (change >0.5D in last year)
Severe Unmanaged Dry Eye Syndrome
Unrealistic Patient Expectations or inability to adapt to blended vision
Advanced Cataract or other significant ocular pathology
Uncontrolled Glaucoma or ocular hypertension
History of Herpes Simplex Keratitis
Autoimmune or Collagen Vascular Diseases
Large Mesopic Pupils (>7.0 mm, relative contraindication for higher dysphotopsia risk)
Amblyopia in either eye (compromises binocularity and functional outcome)

content.explanation:
• Profile: Suitable corneal profile and target add power.
  • Refraction: Stable refraction with moderate presbyopia.
  • Expectations: Realistic and well-counseled.
  • Stable Cornea: No ectasia, adequate thickness.
  • Binocularity: Good binocular function and tolerance to anisometropia.
  • Youthful enthusiasm: Motivated for spectacle independence (implies good neuroadaptation potential).

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Thorough pre-op patient counseling is the most crucial step for managing expectations and ensuring satisfaction.
Pre-existing dry eye must be aggressively managed before surgery to optimize healing and visual outcomes.
A contact lens monovision trial can be a valuable tool to predict patient tolerance to blended vision, though PresbyLASIK often provides a smoother transition.
Neuroadaptation is key; patients need to understand that visual quality will improve over weeks to months.
Patients with higher add powers (e.g., >+2.50D) or significant HOAs pre-op may be less ideal candidates and may benefit more from RLE.
PresbyLASIK does not halt the natural progression of presbyopia; future reading correction may still be required years down the line.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances in PresbyLASIK include more sophisticated and customizable Extended Depth of Focus (EDOF) ablation profiles (e.g., Schwind's 'SmartSurfACE' technology), integration of wavefront-optimized and wavefront-guided treatments for superior optical quality, and improved femtosecond laser platforms for highly precise flap creation. Landmark studies, such as those evaluating Presbyond blended vision, consistently demonstrate high patient satisfaction rates (often 85-95%) and superior binocular uncorrected distance, intermediate, and near visual acuity compared to traditional monovision, with reduced incidence of bothersome dysphotopsia. Research continues to refine treatment algorithms, improve nomograms, and enhance diagnostic capabilities to better predict patient outcomes and identify ideal candidates, with a strong focus on long-term stability and quality of vision.
